sentences.text: Anatalavis rex is known only from two humeri, a right wing and a left wing, which lack the proximal end.
The humerus of Anatalavis rex has a pronounced curve in its shaft, unlike the straight shaft found in the related genus Telmatornis.
The living Anatalavis rex was likely similar in bulk to an average-sized dabbling duck of the genus Anas.
The type species Anatalavis rex was discovered in Hornerstown, New Jersey, with remains collected in 1869 and 1878.
Storrs L. Olson and David C. Parris established the genus Anatalavis in 1987, naming it "duck-winged bird" to reflect its affinity to waterfowl.

The species Anatalavis oxfordi was described by Olson about 80 years after A. rex, based on fossils found in the London Clay Bed A at Walton-on-the-Naze, England, and named after collector Andrew Oxford.
The fossils of Anatalavis rex are likely from the Hornerstown Formation around 66 million years ago, though their exact age relative to the K-Pg boundary is debated due to reworked deposits.
Anatalavis oxfordi is known from a partial skeleton found in the earliest Eocene London Clay, which was well-preserved but delicate and broken.
Jiří Mlíkovský controversially proposed in 2002 that Anatalavis oxfordi should be placed in the separate genus Nettapterornis due to differences in the humerus angle compared to A. rex.
It remains unresolved whether Anatalavis belongs to modern waterfowl or to a basal lineage like Conflictonidae that evolved a filter-feeding beak independently.
A 2019 analysis rejected with some confidence the hypothesis that Anatalavis is closer to living ducks than to the magpie-goose, though it cannot fully exclude this possibility.
